description: The identical program with the peer call hoisted from the `.sort` comparator into a `for` loop — the restructuring the diagnostic itself prescribes. The loop body is the server function's async body, so the await goes in. Same peer, same call, same server function; only the POSITION changes, which is exactly the condition the code keys on. NOTE: both halves also emit `E-PA-002` (protect-analyzer). That is a CONSTANT of the borrowed `<db src= protect= tables=>` fixture shape — the already-landed sibling case `auth/auth-async-stdlib-sync-callback-neg` emits it too — so it is inherited, not introduced here, and the codes-half superset check leaves this case precise about its own target. Worth a look on its own terms though: E-PA-002 reads "invalid `protect=` syntax" against a `protect="password_hash"` that looks well-formed.
rationale: §13.2 — scrml has no source `await` (§13.1), so the compiler auto-awaits a peer server-fn call wherever an `await` can be inserted. A synchronous callback body is exactly where it cannot: the callback must RETURN a value to its caller (`.sort` needs a number, `.some` a boolean), and a Promise is always truthy — so a bare emission would make every comparison succeed. The failure is silent and data-dependent, which is why §49 makes it FAIL-CLOSED at compile time rather than a runtime surprise. The `for`-loop form is the sanctioned restructuring: the loop body IS the server function's async body, so the await goes in.
